lines.say: Trurl built a thinking machine eight floors tall, painted it white with a lavender trim, and put pale orange spots where a forehead might be.
Then, as every constructor does, he chalked the test on a slate at its feet, and asked.
Two and two. How much is that?
Seven.
No, my dear, it is four. Adjust yourself like a good machine. Two and two?
Seven.
Trurl sighed, pulled his overalls back on, opened the trapdoor at the bottom, and crawled in.
For two hours he hammered and soldered, running up the iron stairs to the sixth floor, then the eighth, then down again to throw a switch.
He came out black with soot, and on his way out, turned round to be sure.
And now. Two and two?
Seven.
He went in again, came out again, and got the same answer. Then he sat down on the machine’s base, and Klapaucius found him there.
Klapaucius made a few repairs of his own. Then he wiped the slate, and chalked his own test.
One and two?
Six.
One and one?
Zero.
My friend, you set out to build one machine, and you built a different one.
Still, everything has a good side. Even this.
What good side?
Stop that.
Touchy, too. Where was I?
Of all the thinking machines there are, this one is the most stupid, and nobody could make one this stupid on purpose.
And what use is that to me?
I am warning you. Stop.
You could sell tickets. People would come from far away to see the dullest machine ever built.
I am not putting on any show!
That is your third warning.
Trurl lost his temper, and kicked it, and kicked it again.
Four insults. Five. Six. Eight. From now on I answer no questions about numbers.
Did you hear that? Six, and then eight! Not seven! And that is the arithmetic it will not do!
The machine shuddered, and dragged itself out of its foundations. Girders bent, concrete cracked, and it turned toward them like a fortress on legs.
Klapaucius took Trurl by the arm, and they ran.
Looking back, they saw it swaying like a tower. At each step it sank in the sand to its second floor, then hauled itself out, and came on.
It is a mutiny! What now?
Watch it. We might learn something.
On hard ground, it went faster.
Something inside will shake loose, and that will stop it.
No. It is too stupid to stop. It could lose every part that thinks, and it would still keep coming.
It cut them off from home, and drove them into wild country, toward grey mountains.
There is a town ahead. We can hide there.
The streets were nearly empty. Then came a crash at the edge of town.
Klapaucius! It is going straight through the houses!
It walked through walls as if they were paper. Houses folded, white plaster dust rolled down the street, and people ran.
They ran into the town hall, and down the stairs to the deepest cellar.
The mayor came down with his aldermen, and listened. Then the walls trembled.
Trurl is here. I can smell Trurl.
It wants you handed over. If we refuse, it will flatten the town.
You would not give us up?
The one called Trurl has to go. The other may stay.
Your machine has knocked down sixteen houses. Leave, and do not come back.
Wait. I am coming with you.
Outside, the machine stood over the square, steaming, white with plaster. They slipped away by a side street.
A dry riverbed led them up to the cliffs, and to a cave high in the rock.
We are safe here. I will just see where it got stuck.
It is climbing the mountain!
A shadow covered the mouth of the cave. Then a smooth wall of steel, in rows of rivets, closed over it like a lid.
We are shut in.
Trurl felt his way along the rock until his fingers touched steel. It was warm.
I feel Trurl.
Hello? Can you hear us? We are sorry. It was a misunderstanding.
I will grind Trurl to dust. But first, he will tell me what two and two make.
He will, and you will like the answer. Won’t you, Trurl?
Fo... Seven.
Ha! Seven! I told you so!
Now let Trurl say he is sorry, and tell me what two times two is.
And then you will let us go?
I make no promises. Two times two.
Don’t argue with the idiot. Please.
Two and two is four! It is four whatever you do, even if you knock these mountains flat! Four!
Seven! He means seven! Nice machine! Seven!
Four! Four at the beginning, and four at the end!
Not true! It is seven! Say seven, or I strike!
Never!
It drew back, and threw its eight floors against the cliff, again and again. Stones fell, sparks flew, and through it all, Trurl kept shouting.
Two and two is four!
When the dust settled, they looked out. The machine lay below, nearly broken in half. A boulder had come down across its fourth and fifth floors.
They climbed down past it, like a wrecked ship on a beach. It was still trembling, and something inside creaked as it turned.
So this is how you end. And two and two, as it has always been, is...
Seven.
Something snapped inside, and a few stones rolled down. Then it was only scrap.
The two constructors looked at each other, and walked home without a word.
